ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a common-emitter amplifier. The signal source v_s on the left is connected to the transistor base through the source resistance R_s and coupling capacitor C1; the base also has a bias resistor R_B connected to the +10 V power supply node. The transistor emitter is grounded, the collector is connected to +10 V through R_C, and is connected to the load R_L on the right through the coupling capacitor C2, with the lower end of the load grounded. Reasoning: In the small-signal equivalent circuit, C1 = ∞ indicates that the input coupling capacitor is an AC short circuit, so v_s sees R_s in series with the amplifier input terminal. The +10 V power supply node is AC ground, so R_B is connected from the base to AC ground. The emitter is grounded, and the transistor base input resistance r_pi = β/g_m = 100/0.3861 ≈ 259 Ω, consistent with the given r_a = 259 Ω. Since r_o = ∞, and there is no feedback path from the collector to the base, R_C, R_L, and C2 do not affect the resistance seen by the source at the input terminal. The amplifier input resistance is R_in = R_B || r_pi = 93000 || 259 ≈ 258 Ω. Therefore the total resistance seen by the source v_s is R_s + R_in = 1000 + 258 ≈ 1258 Ω.

method.method_draft: Place a hypothetical test voltage V_test at the v_s terminals and replace the circuit by its AC small-signal form. C1 is short, so after R_s the base node has two shunt paths to AC ground: R_B and r_pi. Compute r_pi = beta/g_m = 100/0.3861 ≈ 259 Ω. Write the base-node equivalent conductance as G = 1/R_B + 1/r_pi, so the shunt resistance is 1/G ≈ 258 Ω. Since any test current from v_s must first pass through R_s and then split through those two shunt paths, the total test resistance is R_s + 1/G = 1000 + 1/(1/93000 + 1/259) ≈ 1258 Ω.
